tracks.tagline: Build an AI agent that reads incoming support tickets, calls tools to look up real information, and decides what to do next — then prove it actually works with evals.

1.title: Your First Tool-Calling LLM Call
1.goal: Get a free LLM API key and make your first tool-calling request: instead of just replying with text, the model decides to call a Python function you defined. This is the core mechanic every agent in this track builds on.
learn: Getting and using a free-tier LLM API key with tool/function-calling support (Google Gemini API or Groq)
Defining a tool schema (name, description, parameters) that the model can call
Reading a tool-call response and executing the matching Python function
Sending the tool's result back to the model for a final answer
steps: Sign up for a free API key from Google AI Studio (Gemini API) or Groq, and confirm the SDK version you install supports function calling.
Create a project folder, install the provider's Python SDK and `python-dotenv`, and store your key in a `.env` file (add it to `.gitignore` immediately).
Write one real tool function, `lookup_order_status(order_id: str) -> dict`, backed by a small hardcoded dictionary of 5-6 fake orders.
Define the tool's JSON schema (name, description, parameter types) in the format your provider expects and pass it to the chat request.
Send a user message like 'What's the status of order A123?' and inspect the raw response to find the tool-call the model wants to make.
Write the glue code that reads the tool name and arguments from the response, calls `lookup_order_status`, and sends the result back as a tool response message.
Print the model's final natural-language answer after it receives the tool result, and confirm it correctly reports the order status.
Commit your code (not `.env`) with a README explaining what a tool call is and how to run the script.
deliverables: A working `lookup_order_status` tool function with sample data
A tool schema definition wired into a chat completion request
Glue code that executes a model-requested tool call and returns the result
A README explaining the tool-calling flow end to end
done_when: Asking about a known order ID returns a correct, tool-grounded answer, not a guess
Asking about an unknown order ID makes the tool return 'not found' and the model reports that honestly
The API key never appears anywhere in committed code or Git history
Printing the raw API response shows a clear tool-call step before the final answer
hints: Tool-calling response shapes differ by provider; read the 'function calling' or 'tool use' section of your provider's docs closely before writing glue code.
Keep the tool's description specific ('Look up the current shipping status of an order by its ID') — vague descriptions make the model call the tool at the wrong times.
The [Gemini function calling docs](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/function-calling) and [Groq tool use docs](https://console.groq.com/docs/tool-use) both have minimal working examples.
1.stretch: Add a second tool, `lookup_customer(email: str)`, and see if the model can chain both tools in one conversation to answer a two-part question.
post_highlights: Made my first tool-calling LLM request where the model chose which function to run
Wired a Python function into an LLM agent's tool-calling loop end to end
Learned how tool schemas and tool responses fit into a real agent request

2.title: Multi-Tool Triage Agent
2.goal: Turn last week's single tool call into a real triage agent that reads a support ticket, classifies it, and calls the right combination of tools to gather context before drafting a reply. This is where 'an LLM that can call one function' becomes 'an agent that reasons about which tools to use.'
learn: Designing a small toolset for one workflow (lookup, classify, escalate)
Writing a system prompt that defines an agent's role, tools, and boundaries
Handling a multi-turn tool-calling loop where the model can call more than one tool per ticket
Structuring ticket data and agent output for a real workflow
steps: Write a `tickets.json` file with 10-15 fake support tickets (subject, body, customer email, order ID where relevant).
Add two more tools: `classify_ticket_category(text: str)` (return `billing`, `shipping`, `bug`, or `other` using simple keyword rules) and `check_refund_eligibility(order_id: str)`.
Write an agent system prompt describing the triage agent's job: read a ticket, gather needed context via tools, then draft a short reply and a suggested category.
Build a loop that keeps calling the model and executing requested tools until the model returns a final (non-tool-call) message, instead of stopping after one round.
Add a safety cap (e.g. max 5 tool-call rounds) so a confused agent cannot loop forever, and log a warning if it hits the cap.
Run the agent over all 10-15 tickets in `tickets.json` and print each ticket's category, tools called, and drafted reply.
Manually review the outputs and fix at least one case where the agent picked the wrong tool or category by adjusting the system prompt or tool descriptions.
Commit your code with a README describing the toolset and the multi-round tool-calling loop.
deliverables: A `tickets.json` file with realistic sample tickets
Three working tools: order lookup, category classification, refund eligibility
A multi-round tool-calling loop with a max-rounds safety cap
A batch run over all sample tickets with printed categories, tool calls and drafted replies
done_when: Running the agent over all sample tickets produces a category and draft reply for each one
At least one ticket in the sample set requires the agent to call two different tools before replying
The safety cap is verified by testing with a deliberately confusing ticket and confirming the loop stops
A previously wrong category or tool choice is fixed and verified after a prompt or description tweak
hints: Keep `classify_ticket_category` simple (keyword matching) for now — the model deciding when to call it is the interesting part this week, not the classifier itself.
Log every tool call with its arguments and result to the console; this is the single most useful debugging habit for agent work.
If the model stops calling tools too early, make the system prompt explicit: 'Always check order and refund status before replying about a refund.'
2.stretch: Add an `escalate_to_human(reason: str)` tool the agent can call for tickets it isn't confident about, and track how often it gets used across your sample set.
post_highlights: Built a multi-tool support ticket triage agent with a real tool-calling loop
Designed a toolset and system prompt so an LLM could gather context before replying
Added a safety cap to prevent runaway tool-calling loops in an autonomous agent

3.title: RAG for Policy-Grounded Replies
3.goal: Give the triage agent a company policy knowledge base so its drafted replies are grounded in real refund/shipping rules instead of the model's guesses. This combines retrieval-augmented generation with the tool-calling loop from Week 2 into one working agent.
learn: Chunking and embedding a small internal knowledge base
Exposing retrieval as a callable tool (`search_policy_docs`) rather than a fixed pre-step
Combining RAG with tool-calling in a single agent loop
Grounding generated text in retrieved context and citing the source
steps: Write 4-6 short policy documents as `.txt` files (e.g. `refund_policy.txt`, `shipping_policy.txt`, `escalation_policy.txt`) with concrete rules.
Write a `chunk_text` function and embed every chunk once, caching vectors to a JSON file keyed by a hash of the chunk.
Write a `search_policy_docs(query: str, top_k=3)` function using cosine similarity, and expose it to the model as a tool alongside Week 2's tools.
Update the system prompt to instruct the agent to call `search_policy_docs` before drafting any reply that mentions a refund, deadline, or policy rule.
Update the drafted-reply output format to include which policy chunk(s) were used, so every policy claim is traceable.
Run the agent over the sample tickets again and check that refund/shipping-related replies now cite real chunk content instead of generic language.
Test a ticket asking about a policy that doesn't exist in your docs and confirm the agent says it cannot confirm rather than inventing a rule.
Commit your code with an updated README describing the policy knowledge base and how retrieval fits into the tool-calling loop.
deliverables: 4-6 policy documents forming a small internal knowledge base
A `search_policy_docs` retrieval tool with cached embeddings
An updated agent that calls retrieval before drafting policy-related replies
Replies that show which policy chunk(s) grounded each claim
done_when: A refund-related ticket produces a reply that correctly cites a real rule from `refund_policy.txt`
A question about a policy not covered by any document gets an honest 'cannot confirm' response instead of a fabricated rule
Re-running the agent does not re-embed the policy documents from scratch (cache is used)
At least 3 sample tickets show retrieval being called before the reply is drafted
hints: Keep chunks reasonably small (200-400 words) so `search_policy_docs` returns focused, relevant text rather than whole documents.
It's fine for retrieval to be 'just another tool' the model chooses to call — you do not need to force it before every single ticket, only policy-related ones.
If citations look wrong, print the retrieved chunks alongside the final reply to check whether retrieval or generation is at fault.
3.stretch: Add a `top_k` sensitivity test: compare retrieved chunks and reply quality at `top_k=1` vs `top_k=3` on 3 tricky tickets.
post_highlights: Built a policy knowledge base and exposed retrieval as a callable tool in an AI agent
Combined RAG with tool-calling so agent replies cite real, retrieved policy rules
Verified the agent gives an honest 'cannot confirm' answer instead of fabricating policy

4.title: API, Evals and Guardrails
4.goal: Wrap the triage agent in a small API, write an evaluation set to measure how often it triages correctly, and add guardrails so it fails safely. This is the engineering polish that turns a working prototype into something you could hand to another team.
learn: Exposing an agent as an HTTP endpoint with a lightweight framework (FastAPI or Flask)
Writing an evaluation set with expected categories and required policy citations
Measuring agent accuracy and tool-call correctness against ground truth
Adding guardrails: input validation, rate limiting basics, and safe failure modes
steps: Install FastAPI (or Flask) and build a `POST /triage` endpoint that accepts a ticket JSON body and returns the agent's category, drafted reply, and tools used.
Add input validation (reject empty subject/body) and wrap the full agent call in `try`/`except` so a tool failure or API timeout returns a clear error response instead of a 500 crash.
Create an `eval_tickets.json` with at least 10 tickets, each with an expected category and, where relevant, an expected policy topic that should be cited.

Write `evaluate.py` that runs every eval ticket through `/triage` (or the agent function directly), checks the category matches and the right policy topic was retrieved, and prints a pass/fail summary with an overall accuracy percentage.
Add a guardrail: if the agent's category confidence is low or it calls zero tools on a policy-related ticket, force an `escalate_to_human` outcome rather than guessing.
Run the eval, find at least one failing case, and fix it (prompt tweak, tool description tweak, or added policy chunk), then re-run to confirm improvement.
Add basic request logging (ticket ID, category, tools called, timestamp) to a local log file for later review.
Write a full README covering setup, running the API, running the eval script, and known limitations, then record a 30-60 second demo of a ticket being triaged end to end.
deliverables: A `POST /triage` API endpoint wrapping the full agent
Input validation and safe error handling on the endpoint
An `eval_tickets.json` set and `evaluate.py` script reporting accuracy
A guardrail that escalates low-confidence or under-grounded triage decisions
done_when: `POST /triage` with a real ticket body returns a category, reply and tool trace within a reasonable time
A deliberately malformed request (empty body) returns a clean error, not a crash
`python evaluate.py` runs at least 10 checks and reports an overall accuracy percentage
A ticket engineered to be low-confidence or ungrounded is escalated instead of answered with a guess
hints: Keep the API thin — it should call the same agent function your eval script calls, so you are testing the real code path, not a duplicate.
An eval accuracy number only means something if you also read a few failing transcripts by hand; don't optimize blindly against the score.
The [FastAPI docs](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com) 'first steps' page has a minimal working endpoint you can adapt directly.
4.stretch: Add a `/triage/batch` endpoint that accepts a list of tickets and returns results with total latency and per-ticket timing, useful for a simple load check.
post_highlights: Wrapped my AI triage agent in a FastAPI endpoint with input validation and error handling
Built an evaluation suite that measures triage accuracy against ground-truth tickets
Added a guardrail that escalates low-confidence tickets instead of letting the agent guess
